b: Parasites are organisms that live in or on a human host and cause harm. They include protozoa (single-celled) and helminths (worms).
Malaria — extra detail because it is important:

Malaria is transmitted by the bite of a female Anopheles mosquito. The Plasmodium parasite enters the red blood cells and destroys them, causing the characteristic fever. There are four main species: - Plasmodium falciparum — most dangerous
Prevention of malaria: - Insecticide-treated bed nets - Indoor residual spraying - Prophylactic drugs for travellers (Doxycycline, Atovaquone-Proguanil)

qs.q: Which parasitic infection could result in strabismus?
qs.e: Ocular toxocariasis caused by Toxocara canis larvae can lead to visual impairment, strabismus, and retinal damage.

qs.q: A 40-year-old man has a peripheral blood eosinophil count of 4500/microliter persisting for 6 months. He has no parasitic infection, no allergic disease, and no drug exposure. Bone marrow shows eosinophilic hyperplasia. FISH reveals FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene. Most likely diagnosis?
o: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis with IgE elevation
qs.e: Persistent marked eosinophilia + FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene = eosinophilic leukemia. This is a clonal myeloid neoplasm driven by a tyrosine kinase fusion. Unlike reactive eosinophilia, it has a primary clonal driver and responds to imatinib.

qs.q: Which blood cell type is primarily responsible for defence against parasitic infections?
qs.e: Eosinophils contain cytotoxic granule proteins (e.g., major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein) specifically effective against helminths and other parasites.
qs.s: Haematology Exam MCQs: Anemia, Leukemia, Coagulation Prep — Hematopathology III

qs.q: Which white blood cell is the primary mediator in parasitic infections and allergic reactions?
qs.e: Eosinophils degranulate against parasites and release mediators in allergic responses; eosinophilia is a hallmark of both conditions.

qs.q: Parasitic infections (trichinosis, schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis) cause elevated numbers of?
qs.e: Tissue-invasive parasites trigger Th2 immune responses and IgE production, driving eosinophilia.
qs.s: Haematopathology MCQs: Blood Disorders, Lymphoma & Anemia

qs.q: Which blood cell type is primarily responsible for defence against parasitic infections and also plays a role in allergic reactions?
qs.e: Eosinophils are granulocytes that are particularly effective against parasitic infections and release mediators that contribute to allergic inflammation.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - July 3, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which of the following cell types is primarily involved in host defense against parasitic infections and allergic reactions?
qs.e: Eosinophils are granulocytes that play a key role in defense against parasitic helminths (worms) and are also heavily involved in allergic and asthmatic responses.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Cellular Immunology Exam - March 27, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which immunoglobulin is associated with immediate hypersensitivity reactions and defense against parasitic infections, primarily by binding to Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils?
qs.e: IgE antibodies are strongly associated with allergic reactions (Type I hypersensitivity) and play a role in immunity against parasites. They bind with high affinity to Fc receptors (FcεRI) on mast cells and basophils.

ai.title: Parasitic Infections
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Parasitic infections are common in East Africa, presenting with fever, anaemia, diarrhoea or eosinophilia. Clinical reasoning hinges on history, simple tests and empirical treatment when investigations are limited.

sections.p: Parasites are organisms that live in or on humans, causing disease through mechanical damage, toxin release or immune activation. In low‑resource settings, malaria, schistosomiasis, soil‑transmitted helminths and protozoal diarrhoea dominate.
Protozoa are single‑cell, often motile; helminths are multicellular worms with specialised tissues. Life cycles involve intermediate hosts or environmental stages.
b: Plasmodium: erythrocytic schizogony; Schistosoma: cercariae penetrate skin; Ascaris: eggs passed in stool, hatch in gut

t.b: Identify parasite morphology in blood, stool or tissue; confirms species and guides treatment

sections.p: Transmission routes vary: mosquito bite for malaria, skin contact with contaminated water for schistosomiasis, ingestion of contaminated food or soil for helminths, and faecal–oral for protozoa.
b: Malaria: Anopheles mosquito → blood stage → liver stage → relapse

t.b: Detects Plasmodium antigens; positive = treat with artemisinin‑based combination

sections.p: Clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic carriage to severe anaemia, organ failure or death. Key presentations: fever with chills, anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly, diarrhoea, eosinophilia.
b: Malaria: fever, rigors, anaemia, cerebral complications

t.b: Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, eosinophilia; helps gauge severity

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, rely on history, simple microscopy, RDTs and basic labs. When unavailable, empirical treatment guided by epidemiology is acceptable.
b: Microscopy of blood smear for malaria

t.b: Detects parasites; confirms species and parasitaemia level; high parasitaemia = severe disease
Identify ova of Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris; presence indicates infection
Positive indicates exposure; not always available

sections.p: Treat the causative organism, provide supportive care and address complications. Prevention focuses on vector control, sanitation and mass drug administration.

t.b: First‑line for Plasmodium falciparum; effective, low resistance in East Africa
Single dose for schistosomiasis; safe in pregnancy
Treats Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris; safe in pregnancy

sections.p: Remember that severe malaria presents with high parasitaemia (>5%) and may need parenteral artesunate. Schistosomiasis can cause portal hypertension; look for splenomegaly and ascites. Soil‑transmitted helminths often present with anaemia and eosinophilia.
b: If RDT negative but clinical suspicion high, repeat smear or treat empirically

t.b: Rule out pulmonary helminths (e.g., Strongyloides) in immunocompromised

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL), altered sensorium, persistent vomiting, jaundice, haemoglobinuria, shock

faq.q: Why is malaria still a problem in East Africa?
faq.a: High vector density, limited bed‑net coverage and emerging drug resistance keep malaria endemic.

faq.q: How do you differentiate malaria from typhoid fever?
faq.a: Malaria shows parasitaemia on smear/RDT; typhoid has Widal titre, but both can present with fever and abdominal pain.

faq.q: What is the first step if a patient has eosinophilia and chronic diarrhoea?
faq.a: Consider helminthic infection; start albendazole and investigate stool ova/cysts.
